title: Different faces of false: The spread and curtailment of false information in the black Panther Twitter discussion
screen_reason: Case study of the #BlackPanther Twitter conversation that reports a quantitative share with a denominator: tweets involved in any of four false-narrative types make up approximately 2.6% of the collected conversation (Table 1: 154,674 false-narrative tweets vs 5,823,001 other). That is a share of items in a keyword corpus coded as false/misleading, so CONTENT. The rest of the paper (diffusion dynamics, community response, bot scores, network structure) yields no further shares with denominators.

estimates.country: not stated (global Twitter conversation about a U.S. film release)
estimates.date: 8-23 February 2018 (#BlackPanther collection window; origin posts 15-24 February 2018)
estimates.measure_type: % of tweets in the collected #BlackPanther conversation that discussed or shared any of four false/misleading narratives
estimates.value_raw: "approximately 2.6% of the total conversation"; Table 1: All False # Total Tweets = 154,674 vs All Other = 5,823,001 (combined dataset 5,989,967 distinct tweets)
estimates.denominator: the collected Black Panther Twitter conversation: 5,989,967 distinct tweets (including retweets) from the #BlackPanther hashtag collection 8-23 February 2018 plus supplementary keyword collection and the timelines of the 278 origin posters
estimates.definition: the tweet was one of the 303 manually identified false-narrative origin posts (71 Fake Attack, 178 Satire Attack, 8 Fake Scene, 46 Alt-Right) or a retweet, quote or reply to one of them (including retweets of those quotes and replies)
estimates.misinfo_def: "we focus on a total of four types of false or misleading narratives that were shared on Twitter regarding the film" - Fake Attacks (fabricated claims of being physically attacked at screenings, with images taken from other media), Satire Attacks (hyperbolic mockery of the Fake Attack posts), Fake Scenes (photoshopped images of scenes not in the film), and Alt-Right ("the claims that the movie promotes these policies or 'is alt-right' are very misleading")
estimates.source_quote: The total amount of tweets discussing or sharing any of the four false-narrative types make up only approximately 2.6% of the total conversation that we were able to collect.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The authors manually categorized posts into the four narrative types using stated rules (a direct claim that Black Panther was Alt-Right; a claim of a scene that did not occur; hyperbolic/nonsensical language or images to separate Satire Attacks from Fake Attacks). Fake Attack and Satire Attack cases were seeded from 15 news articles (BuzzFeed, Vox) that had already exposed them. No second coder, no inter-coder reliability statistic reported.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALLS an adjudicator should see. (1) The NUMERATOR is not 'false tweets': it is every tweet in a false-narrative thread, including the debunking quotes and replies and their retweets - and the paper itself says 'over 95% of the quotes of and replies to Fake Attack origin posts were negative towards those origin posts', while Fake Attack threads are 88.0% retweets-of-quotes. So 2.6% substantially overstates the share of tweets that actually carried a false claim; the false ORIGIN posts number just 303. Marked borderline for that reason, though it is the paper's own headline share and is stated verbatim. (2) Numerator and denominator come from partly different collection routes: the false-narrative tweets were found with supplementary news-seeded keyword searches and the 278 origin posters' full timelines were added to the corpus, so the denominator is not a clean random sample of the hashtag stream. (3) Table 1's components (154,674 + 5,823,001 = 5,977,675) do not reconcile with the stated 5,989,967 distinct tweets - a 12,292-tweet discrepancy the paper does not explain. (4) breadth = misleading because the aggregate mixes fabrications (Fake Attacks, Fake Scenes) with a merely misleading framing (Alt-Right) and with SATIRE, which is false but not deceptive - many reviewers would exclude satire from a misinformation numerator; excluding Satire Attacks would drop the numerator to roughly 101,722 of the same denominator (not entered, since that is a cross-category recomputation R8 forbids). (5) topic coded 'other' because the corpus is an entertainment/film conversation; 'crime_society' is defensible if the field is meant to describe the false claims themselves (fabricated racially-motivated assaults). (6) No country breakdown anywhere in the paper.
estimates.moderator_quote: The combined dataset contains a total of 5,989,967 distinct tweets (including retweets).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Origin posts as a share of all origin posts (303 false vs 1,157,349 'All Other' origin posts in Table 1, i.e. ~0.026%) would be the cleanest prevalence figure in the paper, but it is not stated anywhere and the denominator would have to be built by summing two categories, which R8 forbids - so no row. Table 1's own '% Total: Origin Posts' entries (0.1%, 0.3%, 0.4%, 69.7%, 0.2%, 19.9%) are within-type composition (origin posts as a share of that narrative's own tweets), not misinformation prevalence. (2) CONCENTRATION was checked and cannot be coded: the paper reports counts, not shares - 'Only 11 origin posts in total (5 Fake Attack, 3 Satire Attack, 3 Fake Scene) received more than 50 retweets each, including one Satire Attack origin post that received 46,371 retweets', '5,182 origin posts not related to the false narratives received over 50 retweets', 8 posts with >50 quotes, 5 with >50 replies, 27 quotes with >50 retweets. R1 requires both a group share of users/sources and their share of activity; only the group counts are given, so the striking skew (a handful of posts carrying nearly all the retweets) is unusable. (3) 'over 95% of the quotes of and replies to Fake Attack origin posts were negative towards those origin posts' is a share of RESPONSES that debunked, not a misinformation share - out of scope. (4) Table 3 gives % news agents (0.0007% of all-false users) and % verified (0.15%) - actor types, not misinformation. (5) Bot-score distributions (Figure 7) are reported only as density histograms, no share above a threshold. (6) Figures 1-8 are images in the source text and could not be read; no value was taken from them. (7) The related-work section cites external figures (48 million Twitter accounts may be bots; two-thirds of shared links shared by bots) - cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8.

rob.design: Single-case observational study of one Twitter conversation. Frame: all tweets containing '#BlackPanther' posted 8-23 February 2018 via the Twitter API, supplemented by keyword/phrase searches derived from 15 news articles to locate Fake Attack and Satire Attack tweets, plus the complete timelines of the 278 users behind the 303 false-narrative origin posts; combined dataset 5,989,967 distinct tweets. Coding procedure: authors manually categorized origin posts into four narrative types with stated linguistic and image criteria; falsity of the Fake Attack narrative rests on journalists' debunking (BuzzFeed, Vox). No second coder, no inter-coder reliability statistics, no sampling weights, no response rate (not a survey). Bot likelihood from CMU Bot-Hunter, verified status from the Twitter API, news-agent status from a known handle list. Generalizability is explicitly limited by the authors to this one conversation.
